pages.text: The Old Photograph

image.note: Cover: a boy holding a faded photo, an old mango tree behind

pages.text: Contents. The Photograph / Nobody Knows / Nana Remembers / The Gateman's Secret / The Land Before / The History Keeper.

The photograph fell out of the old book like a secret. Okon caught it as it drifted down: a small, square, faded picture, brown with age, of a place he had never seen. Green fields. A great tree. A young man and woman, smiling. And behind them, empty land where Okon knew, absolutely knew, his own home now stood.

image.note: Okon catching a faded old photograph

pages.text: Okon had only borrowed the book from the community room shelf, a dusty old thing nobody read. But the photograph inside it was far more interesting than any book. He turned it over. On the back, in faded ink, were four words: Home, before it changed. That was all. No names. No date. Just a mystery, in his hands.

image.note: Okon examining the back of the photo

pages.text: He studied the picture until he knew every corner. The fields. The winding path. And the tree, an enormous mango tree, heavy with fruit, standing right in the middle of it all. Okon frowned. He knew a mango tree exactly like that. There was one on the estate, right now, old and huge, that dropped fruit on the cars. Could it be the same tree?

image.note: The photo's mango tree beside the estate's mango tree

pages.text: It made no sense. The estate was flats and roads and gates and cars. The photo was fields and a path and open sky. They could not be the same place. And yet there was the tree, the very same crooked branch, in both. Okon decided, then and there, to solve it. Somebody, somewhere on the estate, had to know.

image.note: Okon determined, holding the photo up to the light

pages.text: He asked the other children first. Nobody knew. He asked their parents. Nobody knew either. "The estate has always been here," they shrugged. "Flats and roads, as long as we have lived." But that was just it, Okon thought. As long as they had lived. The photo was older than any of them. He needed someone older still.

image.note: Okon asking puzzled parents and children

pages.text: Two people on the estate were older than anyone. One was Nana, the grandmother of them all, who sat in her green chair by her window and knew everybody's name. The other was Remigius, the quiet gateman, who had stood at that gate longer than most residents had been alive. Okon took his photograph, and went first to Nana.

image.note: Okon setting off with the photo, gate and green chair in view

pages.text: Nana took the little photograph in her old hands, and held it a long, long time, and did not speak. Okon waited, hardly breathing. At last she looked up, and her eyes were bright and wet. "Where," she said softly, "did you find this? I have not seen this picture in sixty years."

image.note: Nana gazing at the photo, moved, in her green chair

pages.text: "You know it?" cried Okon. "Know it," said Nana, and laughed, a small, amazed laugh. "Child, I am in it." She turned the photo so he could see, and pointed a trembling finger at the young woman in the green fields, smiling beside the young man under the mango tree. "That," she said, "is me. And that is your estate, long before it was an estate at all."

image.note: Nana pointing at her young self in the photo

pages.text: "This was all farmland," said Nana, "our family's farm, long ago, before the roads and the flats, when I was a girl no older than your sister. We grew maize here, and yams, and under that mango tree we ate our lunch every single day. Then the estate was built, and the fields went, all of them."

image.note: A memory: young Nana and family farming the land

pages.text: "All of them," said Okon slowly, "except the tree." Nana smiled. "Except the tree. When they built the estate, I begged them to leave the old mango tree standing. And they did. Every day I see it from this window, and I remember the fields, and the girl I was, and everyone who is gone. It is the last living thing from that whole world."

image.note: Nana at her window, looking out at the mango tree

pages.text: But there was still the young man in the photo, smiling beside young Nana, and Okon had to know. "Nana," he asked, "who is he?" Nana looked, and her face grew soft. "That," she said, "was a boy who worked our farm. A good boy, younger than me, who loved this land as much as I did, and never, ever left it. Go and show him the photo, Okon. He is still here."

image.note: Nana pointing to the young man, a knowing smile

pages.text: Okon ran to the gate, the photo in his hand, and there stood Remigius, the quiet gateman, as he stood every day, greeting cars, opening the gate, saying little. Okon held up the photograph. "Mr Remigius," he said, "is this... is this you?" The old gateman took the photo, and went very still, and for a moment the busy gate and the passing cars all seemed to fall away.

image.note: Okon showing the photo to Remigius at the gate

pages.text: "It is me," said Remigius at last, very quietly. "A long time ago. On this land, when it was green." He looked up at the flats, the roads, the cars, as if seeing straight through them to the fields underneath. "They built all this," he said, "and I could not leave. So I stayed, at the gate, on the only patch of the old farm still mine to stand on. Sixty years at this gate, and nobody ever asked me why."

image.note: Remigius holding the photo, gazing at the estate

pages.text: Okon looked at the quiet gateman he had walked past a thousand times without a thought, and saw him, suddenly, completely differently. Not just the man who opened the gate. The man who had been here longest of all. The keeper of the estate's whole forgotten history, standing at the door, unnoticed, for sixty years.

image.note: Okon seeing Remigius anew, with new respect

pages.text: "Tell me," said Okon. "Tell me all of it." And Remigius, who almost never spoke, told him: of the farm, and the harvests, and young Nana and her family, and the great mango tree, and the day the builders came, and how the fields became flats, and how a young man who had lost his whole world chose to guard its gate rather than leave it behind. Okon listened to every word.

image.note: Remigius telling the story, Okon rapt

pages.text: "Does anyone else know?" Okon asked. Remigius shook his head. "They pass me every day. They see a gateman. They do not see the land under their feet, or the farm that was, or the boy in the photograph." "It is not gone," said Okon fiercely. "You are still here. Nana is still here. The tree is still here. It is not gone at all."

image.note: Okon insisting, Remigius touched

pages.text: Okon could not keep such a thing to himself, and he did not think he should. With Nana's blessing and Remigius's shy permission, he took the story to the Tafiya Times, the estate's own newspaper, and Itohan put it on the front page: THE LAND BEFORE TAFIYA, and the little faded photograph, printed for the whole estate to see.

image.note: The newspaper front page with the old photo

pages.text: The estate was amazed. Neighbours who had lived there for years, who had walked past the gate and the green chair a thousand times, learned for the first time whose land they lived on, and who had kept its memory all along. People stopped at the gate now, not just to pass through, but to talk to Remigius, and to listen.

image.note: Neighbours gathered at the gate, talking with Remigius

pages.text: Under the old mango tree, the estate put up a small sign, made by the children, that told the truth of the place: that here, once, were green fields and a family farm; that this tree had shaded their lunches; and that two people who remembered it, Nana and Remigius, were living still among them. History, Okon thought, was not only in books. Sometimes it sat in a green chair, or stood at a gate.

image.note: The children's sign under the mango tree

pages.text: Nana kept the photograph after that, in a frame by her window, where she could see both the picture and the tree at once, the fields that were, and the tree that remained. And Okon, whenever he passed the gate, would stop, and greet Remigius by name, and sometimes stay to listen, for he had learned the estate's best-kept secret: the most important people are often the ones we walk straight past.

image.note: Okon greeting Remigius warmly at the gate

pages.text: The Old Photograph. Okon, who solved the mystery of the land. Nana, who was a girl in the green fields. Remigius, the gateman who kept the whole story at his post for sixty years. And the mango tree, the last living thing from a world that is gone, but not forgotten. A reminder: every place has a history, and sometimes it is standing right in front of you.

image.note: Nana, Remigius, Okon, and the mango tree together
